About: Dipole in a Uniform Field — All Torque, No Force

Source

Topic
Electric dipole in a uniform external field
Concept
In a uniform field the net force on a dipole is exactly zero; the two equal-and-opposite forces form a couple, so the dipole rotates on the spot.
Level
JEE / NCERT Class 12 electrostatics.
Standard result
τ = p × E (magnitude pE sin θ); U = −p · E (= −pE cos θ). Stable equilibrium at θ = 0, unstable at θ = 180°.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A dipole between two forces

A tiny dipole sits in a uniform electric field — the arrows are all the same length and all point the same way. The field pulls the +q charge one way and the −q charge exactly the opposite way, with exactly the same strength.

Predict: when you release the dipole, what does it do?

2 · Watch the couple act

Press ▶ Play. Track the red and blue force arrows on the two charges — they stay equal in length and opposite in direction at every instant. The centre of the dipole (the centre dot) does not move; only the orientation changes. The dipole swings toward alignment, overshoots, and oscillates about θ = 0.

Read the sidebar: net force = 0 N, exactly, at every angle. Nothing pushes the dipole sideways.

3 · The energy curve

Below the scene, the curve U(θ) = −pE cos θ shows the potential energy. The moving dot is the dipole's current state on that curve.

Where does the dipole want to settle?

4 · The other equilibrium — 180°

At θ = 180° the dipole is anti-aligned: +q points against E, −q along E. The torque here is also zero — sin 180° = 0.

Set the angle to 179° — a hair off perfect anti-alignment — and release. What happens?

5 · Explore

Try:

• Change E — the couple gets stronger, so the dipole swings faster.
• Change p — the couple's arm gets longer, so torque grows.
• Set the angle to 90° and release — τ is at its maximum.
• Set the angle to 179° — a hair from the peak — and watch it fall away.

Whatever you do, the net force stays exactly 0 N and the centre dot never moves. That is the whole lesson.

01

At a glance

An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges a small distance apart. Here it sits in a uniform electric field, one with the same strength and direction everywhere. The sim shows the field, the dipole, the force on each charge, and a curve of the dipole's potential energy.

What you'll learn

  • How to find the total force and the torque on a dipole in a field.
  • How the dipole's potential energy depends on its angle.
  • Which orientations are equilibria, and whether each one is stable.
The dipole moment p points from −q to +q. The angle θ is measured from p to the field E.

What's on screen

  • Field E: the amber arrows, all alike.
  • Force on +q: the red arrow at the positive charge.
  • Force on −q: the blue arrow at the negative charge.
  • Dipole moment p: the arrow from −q to +q.
See itOpen the sim at its starting values. Watch for: the dipole tilted at θ = 60° to the field, with a red and a blue arrow on its charges.

03

In a uniform field the net force is zero

The field pushes the +q charge along E with force qE. It pushes the −q charge against E with force −qE. The two forces have equal size and opposite directions, wherever the dipole points:

Fnet = qE + (−qE) = 0
This needs the field to be the same at both charges.

Each charge is still pushed, but the dipole's centre feels no net push. It does not accelerate along any direction. At the starting values each force is qE = 4 nC × 2000 V/m = 8.0×10⁻⁶ N. The charges sit d = p/q = 1.5 cm apart, and the net force reads 0 N exactly at every angle.

See itKeep θ = 60° and let it run. Watch for: 0 N (exact) for the net force, arrows of equal length pointing opposite ways, and the centre dot staying put.
04

The pair of forces makes a torque pE sin θ

Two equal and opposite forces along different lines make a couple. They cannot move the centre, but they turn the dipole. Each charge sits d/2 from the centre, and only the part of its force perpendicular to the dipole axis turns it. That part is qE sin θ. The torque is the sum for both charges:

τ = p × E    |τ| = qE·d·sin θ = pE sin θ
The torque turns p toward E.

So the torque is zero when p is parallel or antiparallel to E, and largest when they are perpendicular. At θ = 60° it is 1.04×10⁻⁷ N·m. At θ = 90° it reaches pE = 6×10⁻¹¹ × 2000 = 1.20×10⁻⁷ N·m. Doubling E or p doubles it. The readout shows |τ|, without its sign.

See itSet θ = 90° and pause. Watch for: p at right angles to the field, and a torque reading of 1.20×10⁻⁷ N·m.
05

The potential energy is −pE cos θ

Turning the dipole against the torque takes work, and that work is stored as potential energy. Counting U as zero at θ = 90°, the energy depends only on the angle:

U = −p·E = −pE cos θ
The curve below the scene plots this, and the dot marks the present angle.

U is lowest at θ = 0°, where it is −pE = −1.20×10⁻⁷ J, and highest at θ = 180°, where it is +1.20×10⁻⁷ J. The full swing is 2pE = 2.40×10⁻⁷ J. Released at 60°, with U = −6.00×10⁻⁸ J, the dipole speeds up as U falls. It gains 6.0×10⁻⁸ J of kinetic energy by the time it passes θ = 0°. Nothing damps it, so it swings between +60° and −60° for ever.

See itSet θ = 0° and pause. Watch for: the dot at the bottom of the energy curve, −1.20×10⁻⁷ J, and stable (min U) under Equilibrium.
06

0° is stable and 180° is unstable

The torque is zero at both θ = 0° and θ = 180°, so both are equilibria. They differ in what a small nudge does. Near 0° the torque −pE sin θ points back toward 0°, so the dipole oscillates about it. For small swings the period is T = 2π√(I/pE), which is 1.15 s at the starting values.

At 180°, U is a maximum. A small push to θ = 180° − δ gives a torque that points away from 180°, so the angle grows and the dipole falls toward 0°. Without damping it overshoots to the far side and climbs back. Energy explains it: a hill top is an equilibrium, but not a stable one.

See itSet θ = 179° and press Play. Watch for: almost no motion at first, then a quick swing through 0° and on to the far side, again and again. The starting torque is only 2.09×10⁻⁹ N·m.
07

Where it matters

  • Polar molecules. Water has a permanent dipole moment of about 6×10⁻³⁰ C·m. In an applied field its molecules turn to line up with it.
  • Microwave ovens. The field reverses direction billions of times a second, so the torque keeps turning water molecules back and forth. Their motion heats the food.
  • Non-uniform fields. If the field differs between the two charges, the forces no longer cancel and a net force appears too. That is why a charged comb attracts small bits of paper.
  • Limits of the sim. The field is uniform, nothing damps the motion, and the moment of inertia is fixed. The values of p are far larger than those of real molecules.
08

Summary

In one line. The torque on a dipole and its potential energy both depend on the angle θ between p and E.

Key points

  • In a uniform field, Fnet = 0 and τ = pE sin θ turns the dipole.
  • U = −pE cos θ: the minimum at 0° is stable, the maximum at 180° is unstable.

Common mix-ups

  • "Zero net force means nothing happens." The forces cancel, but they act at different points, so the dipole turns.
  • "Zero torque means stable." The torque is zero at 180° too, but a tiny nudge grows there.
  • "The field pulls the dipole along it." That needs a non-uniform field. A uniform one only rotates.

Things to try on your own

  • Predict the 90° torque for E = 3000 V/m and p = 10 ×10⁻¹¹ C·m, then check it.
  • Release from 120° and compare the swing with the one from 60°.
